description_full: Hubbell Incorporated, together with its subsidiaries, manufactures and sells electrical and utility solutions in the United States and internationally. It operates through two segments, Electrical Solutions and Utility Solutions. The Utility Solution segment offers critical components that allow the grid to transmit and distribute energy, as well as the communications and controls technologies, including utility transmission and distribution components, such as arresters, insulators, connectors, anchors, bushings, enclosures, cutouts, and switches; and solutions that serve the edge of the utility infrastructure comprising smart meters, communications systems, and protection and control devices. It sells its products under various brands and/or trademarks to the electrical distribution, substation and transmission markets, as well as markets for grid protection and controls, utility meters and advanced metering infrastructure and telcom and gas distribution markets. The Electrical Solution segment offers standard and special application wiring device products, rough-in electrical products, connector and grounding products, and other electrical equipment for use in industrial, commercial, and institutional facilities by electrical contractors, maintenance personnel, electricians, utilities, and telecommunications companies. It also designs and manufactures various industrial controls, and communication systems for use in the non-residential and industrial markets, as well as in the oil and gas, and mining industries. This segment sells its products through electrical and industrial distributors, home centers, retail and hardware outlets, and residential product-oriented internet sites; and special application products primarily through wholesale distributors to contractors, industrial customers, and original equipment manufacturers. The company was founded in 1888 and is headquartered in Shelton, Connecticut.

financial_summary: Hubbell Inc is a large-cap industrials business with a $22.9B market cap on $5.8B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +6% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 19% against a 9% cost of capital — a 10-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 32%.

The business throws off $875M in free cash flow — roughly 15 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.16× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.3× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage runs at 8.8×.

Shareholder yield of 2.4% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 1.9× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

Tariff and trade-policy exposure — industrial exporters sit squarely in the crosshairs of protectionist policy, and retaliatory tariffs can close markets without warning.

sect: Its 21% operating margin runs 12pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.85x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.1% of sector revenue and 0.3% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+4.9% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 550 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 23% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 33% and a beta of 0.97, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $228.5M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 42% in the 2020 crash, 17% in the 2022 bear market and 54% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $319 (margin of safety -36%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 24%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $160 to $627 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Industrials peers: EV/EBITDA 17.4 vs 13.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 26% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.8% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.3% (vs the 8% bar).
The 13 covering analysts target $534 on average, 23% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 19% clears the cost of capital of 9.1% by 10pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have been steady (CV 0.17).
It runs a 32% gross margin and converts 15% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.16x.
ROE of 23% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.1x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 5pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 0.6% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 1.3x net debt to EBITDA ($497.9M of cash against $2.3B of debt), with interest covered 8.8x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 5.2, in the safe zone).
Goodwill makes up 37% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 5.7% over 3 years, 6.9% over 5 years and 5.6% over 10 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 23% of profits supports about 4.2% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 9.3% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.8x depreciation (2.7% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 21, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.4%), and institutions hold 98%.
It returns 2.4% a year to shareholders (1.0% in buybacks and 1.4% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 41 consecutive years, raising it 8.5% a year over the last five.
people: With about 19,600 employees, each generates about $298K of revenue, 0.8x the Industrials median, and revenue has grown 5.7% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $45K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.7M (9x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
